title: Trump Claims a Secret Oil Mission Moved 100 Million Barrels Through Hormuz. His Energy Secretary Says He Knows Nothing.
excerpt: The contradiction between the president and his own cabinet underscores the opacity of the Strait of Hormuz situation — and India, which imports 85% of its crude, needs clarity more than anyone
body:
President Donald Trump told reporters on Wednesday that the United States had secretly moved "millions of barrels" of Iranian oil out of circulation and directed a covert military mission that helped more than 100 million barrels of crude transit the Strait of Hormuz safely. Hours later, his own Energy Secretary told Congress he knew nothing about it.

The contradiction, which played out across a White House press gaggle and a congressional hearing in the same afternoon, has added a new layer of uncertainty to a situation that India — the world's third-largest oil importer — cannot afford to misread.

## What Trump Said

Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump claimed the US had been quietly extracting Iranian oil for weeks. "Every night, we took that oil," he said. "Millions of barrels of oil has come out, and that's why it's at $85-90 a barrel instead of $250."

He followed up on Truth Social, saying he had directed a secret military operation last month to support oil tankers and commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz that had resulted in "more than 100 MILLION Barrels of Oil making its way through the Straight, and into the Open Market." He claimed more than 200 ships had made their way through the waterway.

## What His Energy Secretary Said

On the same day, Energy Secretary Chris Wright testified before the House Science, Space and Technology Committee. Asked about the president's claim that the US had taken millions of barrels of oil out of Iran, Wright said plainly: "I'm not aware of that."

Wright did acknowledge that the US military had "helped get some oil out of the Strait of Hormuz" and that ship traffic through the waterway had risen "very meaningfully" over the past week. He also confirmed that nearly 100 vessels had used the administration's Jones Act waiver, which allows foreign-built ships to carry oil between US ports — a measure designed to increase domestic supply flexibility during the crisis.

But the gap between Trump's sweeping claim and Wright's measured testimony was hard to miss.

## Why It Matters for India

India imports roughly 85% of its crude oil, and before the conflict began, three-quarters of all crude transiting the Strait of Hormuz was bound for Asia, with China and India together accounting for 44% of total exports through the waterway.

The truth about Hormuz throughput is not academic for New Delhi. Every additional barrel that gets through lowers the pressure on Indian refiners, eases the rupee, and reduces the ballooning energy subsidy bill that has pushed India's fiscal deficit toward 4.8% of GDP.

Global oil reserves have fallen to their lowest level since 2003, according to a Livemint analysis of EIA data. The IEA's coordinated release of 400 million barrels from member countries' emergency stocks in March — the largest in the agency's history — has been drawn down significantly. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve now holds 349.2 million barrels, its lowest since August 2023. The Department of Energy is trying to loan another 40 million barrels to energy companies.

Alternative routes exist — Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline can carry up to 7 million barrels per day, and the UAE's Habshan-Fujairah pipeline adds 1.8 million. But the IEA estimates available alternative export capacity at only 3.5 to 5.5 million barrels per day, a fraction of Hormuz's pre-war throughput of 20 million.

## The Market Shrug

Markets appear to have decided that the direction of travel matters more than the details. Brent crude fell below $89 on Friday morning — a near two-month low — after Trump cancelled planned strikes on Iran and said a peace deal could be signed as soon as this weekend. Asian equities rallied. The rupee was expected to open stronger, in the 95.25-95.30 range against the dollar.

But analysts urge caution. ING Bank said in a note Friday: "We would be cautious about assuming that the extension of the ceasefire is a done deal. Even if it is, it could be fragile. And clearly, if nuclear talks do not progress, it could very easily fall apart."

For India, the numbers are unforgiving. Hormuz throughput fell by nearly 6 million barrels per day in Q1 2026 — a 30% collapse compared with a year earlier. Whether 100 million barrels have genuinely transited the Strait under US military escort, or whether Trump's claim is an exaggeration of a smaller operation, the Strait remains the single most important chokepoint for India's energy security.

India's refiners have quietly secured supply through August. Its diplomats are preparing for a tense G7 meeting. Its markets are rallying on hope. But hope is not a strategy for a country that burns 5.5 million barrels of oil a day. The truth about what is getting through Hormuz — and how much of it is headed for Indian ports — is the question that everything else depends on.
